compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: this section shows how the same evidence gets read with different emphasis; it is not a way of choosing people by type. Reviews, probation decisions and promotion scores should never be awarded by type, and type says nothing about who is more competent.

### INFP and INTJ: the first look at a portfolio

(Fictional scene) One portfolio, with three drafts, a page of the author's own statement and a revision log. One reviewer may look first at what changed between drafts, circle the shift from representation to collage, and ask which moment made the earlier approach worth abandoning; the other may look first at the rhythm of the final version, point out that two pages in the middle say the same thing, and ask whether they can become one.

The two notice different evidence in the same material. The first reads the traces of choice: what was given up behind each change, whether one version was pushed along by someone else; the follow-up question is usually "what did you give up". The second reads structural coherence: whether the main line is single, whether every page advances it, whether removing one page would bring it down; the follow-up is usually "which page could you not lose". Both count, and both are partial — traces alone mistake the number of revisions for effort, structure alone underestimates the hesitation inside the process.

The number of revisions proves nothing by itself: some settle in three drafts, some are still looking for direction after a dozen, with deadline pressure and collaboration conditions in between. Drafts are useful for checking the reasons behind a choice, not for scoring effort.

### INFP and INTJ: a cousin wants to leave banking to illustrate

(Fictional scene) Over dinner, a cousin says she wants to leave her bank job to do illustration. Both receive the same information: six years in the job, savings roughly covering a year of expenses, illustration commissions just starting, and fixed monthly costs she cannot state precisely herself.

Both will ask what she actually wants, and both will reckon the income risk; the weighing lands in different places. One may focus on whether the trial period preserves the direction: take three different kinds of commission first and see which one she still wants to draw after finishing; if only the disliked work remains after a year, the cost of this path has to be recalculated. The other may focus on whether the income assumption can be tested: take commissions through existing channels for three months, record what actually arrives and how long each took, then see whether that figure covers fixed costs.

In the fictional career conversation, the two questions can support the same trial: does the illustration work still appeal once it becomes paid work, and does the income cover the costs the cousin needs to meet? Either person can raise both questions.

The check is small and available to both: ask her to write three lines — how much income she will give up, how long she can go without a result, and the date by which she changes the plan if nothing has moved. If all three can be written, the conversation lands on a plan; if one cannot, it is still on a wish. How she answers and how the two ask cannot be used to infer type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Quietness, a cool style of work, saying little, a messy desk or a perfectly ordered one — none of these is evidence. Both types contain people who keep a room like a show flat, and people whose desk holds three months of takeaway containers. Treating a lifestyle as a type fingerprint is an easy mismatch to make.

The second mismatch turns difference into ability. Saying INTJ is better at decisions and INFP better at empathy sounds like praise, but it converts a position in the model into a level of skill; both stacks describe which kind of information gets handled more often, not how well it is handled.

The third happens in assessment settings: mistaking "like me" for "suitable". The feeling that a piece of work is obviously what we want often means only that it follows a route the reviewer knows. This is especially dangerous in hiring and promotion, which is why this page keeps repeating that type is not a screening tool.

The fourth uses which question comes first as a test. On the same material, either type may ask about intention first, and either may ask about structure first; order is constrained by role, experience and the time available, and cannot be read backwards into a type.

### INFP and INTJ: the first look at a portfolio

(Fictional scene) One portfolio, with three drafts, a page of the author's own statement and a revision log. One reviewer may look first at what changed between drafts, circle the shift from representation to collage, and ask which moment made the earlier approach worth abandoning; the other may look first at the rhythm of the final version, point out that two pages in the middle say the same thing, and ask whether they can become one.

The two notice different evidence in the same material. The first reads the traces of choice: what was given up behind each change, whether one version was pushed along by someone else; the follow-up question is usually "what did you give up". The second reads structural coherence: whether the main line is single, whether every page advances it, whether removing one page would bring it down; the follow-up is usually "which page could you not lose". Both count, and both are partial — traces alone mistake the number of revisions for effort, structure alone underestimates the hesitation inside the process.

The number of revisions proves nothing by itself: some settle in three drafts, some are still looking for direction after a dozen, with deadline pressure and collaboration conditions in between. Drafts are useful for checking the reasons behind a choice, not for scoring effort.
### INFP and INTJ: a cousin wants to leave banking to illustrate

(Fictional scene) Over dinner, a cousin says she wants to leave her bank job to do illustration. Both receive the same information: six years in the job, savings roughly covering a year of expenses, illustration commissions just starting, and fixed monthly costs she cannot state precisely herself.

Both will ask what she actually wants, and both will reckon the income risk; the weighing lands in different places. One may focus on whether the trial period preserves the direction: take three different kinds of commission first and see which one she still wants to draw after finishing; if only the disliked work remains after a year, the cost of this path has to be recalculated. The other may focus on whether the income assumption can be tested: take commissions through existing channels for three months, record what actually arrives and how long each took, then see whether that figure covers fixed costs.

The check is small and available to both: ask her to write three lines — how much income she will give up, how long she can go without a result, and the date by which she changes the plan if nothing has moved. The number of revisions proves nothing by itself: some settle in three drafts, some are still looking for direction after a dozen, with deadline pressure and collaboration conditions in between. Drafts are useful for checking the reasons behind a choice, not for scoring effort.

### INFP and INTJ: a cousin wants to leave banking to illustrate

(Fictional scene) Over dinner, a cousin says she wants to leave her bank job to do illustration. Both receive the same information: six years in the job, savings roughly covering a year of expenses, illustration commissions just starting, and fixed monthly costs she cannot state precisely herself.

Both will ask what she actually wants, and both will reckon the income risk; the weighing lands in different places. One may focus on whether the trial period preserves the direction: take three different kinds of commission first and see which one she still wants to draw after finishing; if only the disliked work remains after a year, the cost of this path has to be recalculated. The other may focus on whether the income assumption can be tested: take commissions through existing channels for three months, record what actually arrives and how long each took, then see whether that figure covers fixed costs.

In the fictional career conversation, the two questions can support the same trial: does the illustration work still appeal once it becomes paid work, and does the income cover the costs the cousin needs to meet? Either person can raise both questions.

The check is small and available to both: ask her to write three lines — how much income she will give up, how long she can go without a result, and the date by which she changes the plan if nothing has moved. If all three can be written, the conversation lands on a plan; if one cannot, it is still on a wish. How she answers and how the two ask cannot be used to infer type.
sections.title: INFP and INTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
Quietness, a cool style of work, saying little, a messy desk or a perfectly ordered one — none of these is evidence. Both types contain people who keep a room like a show flat, and people whose desk holds three months of takeaway containers. Treating a lifestyle as a type fingerprint is an easy mismatch to make.

The second mismatch turns difference into ability. Saying INTJ is better at decisions and INFP better at empathy sounds like praise, but it converts a position in the model into a level of skill; both stacks describe which kind of information gets handled more often, not how well it is handled.

The third happens in assessment settings: mistaking "like me" for "suitable". The feeling that a piece of work is obviously what we want often means only that it follows a route the reviewer knows. This is especially dangerous in hiring and promotion, which is why this page keeps repeating that type is not a screening tool.

The fourth uses which question comes first as a test. On the same material, either type may ask about intention first, and either may ask about structure first; order is constrained by role, experience and the time available, and cannot be read backwards into a type.
sections.title: INFP and INTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two sittings land on INFP and INTJ, resist picking one immediately. Check three things: whether the item bank is the same version, whether the language was the same, and whether you were describing yourself with choices available or yourself as the job requires you to be. All three affect the answers; which one mattered depends on the case and cannot be assumed.

Pick a few comparable decisions where you had room to choose. Note the goal, the constraints and the reasons for each choice. You may find yourself relying on different criteria in different situations. The notes can help you reflect on those changes and cannot establish a type or whether your score was close to a cutoff.
sections.title: INFP and INTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
What differs is which kind of evidence gets cited more, not who looks first or how long they look: one side may ask what the author wants the piece to become, the other whether the main line holds.

Both questions can appear in the same person. Role and task rewrite the emphasis — asked for a conclusion, both will gather the evidence first; doing an initial screen, both may look at the whole. So a single phrase or a single order cannot assign a type; what discriminates better is which kind of evidence recurs across comparable situations.
items.question: Looking at the same piece of work, what evidence does each notice?

items.answer:
The stacks share Fi and Te, but the positions differ. INFP leads with Fi and has Ne as its outward-facing auxiliary. INTJ leads with Ni and has Te as its outward-facing auxiliary.

The shared pair also sits in different seats: Fi is dominant in INFP and third in INTJ. Position describes emphasis inside the model only. It does not follow that one person reflects only after everything else is finished, nor that one person's value judgements arrive later — practice, duty and circumstance all change the expression.
items.question: They share Fi and Te — why do they still read as two different people?

items.answer:
Not by counting revisions or by whether a first draft survives. The number of revisions, and whether a plan gets overturned, depend on the risk in the task, how clear the criteria are and how much time is left; none of that maps one to one onto four letters.

What can be discussed is the reason: across comparable situations, do you redo the work more often because the premise of the main line does not hold, or because the structure is sound but the result does not read like what was meant. Both types have both reasons; the difference is which is reached for first, and one document's history cannot decide a person.
items.question: An INTJ also overturns their own plan, an INFP also ships a first draft — can they still be told apart?

items.answer:
Use them as directions for questions, not as scoring items. One side's questions help the author state the intention; the other's help the author see the structure. Both belong in the feedback.

In practice, write two columns: one for what this material demonstrates, one for what evidence is still missing. If the second column is empty, check first whether a key gap went unrecorded; only judge within the scope the current material supports, and do not conclude that a verdict came too early merely because the column is empty.
items.question: In a portfolio review, how can these two focus points be used without doing harm?

items.answer:
One question any team may need to settle is when to stop exploring options and agree on a version. Either type can welcome more exploration or ask for a deadline, depending on the project.

A workable approach writes the agreement down first: set an end point for exploration and leave one review for revision — before a given point new directions may be added, after it only cuts; if a cut reveals that the main line has collapsed, go back one step and state the reason. Who proposes which clause and who concedes first depends on duty and deadline, not on type.
items.question: Working together, which agreement do they most often get stuck on?

items.answer:
Check the tool and the conditions first, not which set of items explains it: the assessment name, version, language and scoring definition, and whether you were answering as yourself with choices available or as the job requires you to be.

Beyond that, if the tool reports dimension scores, look at the T/F and J/P results against its boundary notes; both sitting close to the boundary only suggests that these two labels are sensitive to changes in answering, and does not establish that the shift came from circumstances. Where no dimension scores or boundary notes are provided, do not infer a near-boundary result and do not prescribe a retest interval.

**Four-position convention on this page**: the arrangement of the four functions, in particular the attitude of the third process, follows a common writing adopted here as an editorial convention. Other sources handle it differently, and this is not presented as the Foundation's only reading.

**Editorial fiction note**: the portfolio review and the conversation about changing careers are fictional examples used to illustrate different ways of weighing a decision, and correspond to no real person or event.

**Scope limits**: assessment results have to be read alongside the item bank, language version and the circumstances of answering. They are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships, and not for predicting whether two people will work well together or be drawn to each other; psychological and clinical judgements belong to qualified professionals.
